paragraphs.text: XV.A. Energy Management
Airplane Flying Handbook Ch. 4
What is it & Why is it Important?
What: Process of controlling altitude and airspeed to maintain safe and efficient flight
Why: Critical to flight safety and essential for basic & advanced airmanship skills
Prevent loss of control in flight (LOC-I), controlled flight into terrain (CFIT), approach/landing accidents
Essential for maintaining vertical flight paths & airspeed profiles and transitioning between profiles
Ex. Final approach, constant airspeed climbs, or leveling off from a descent
The Airplane as an Energy System
An aircraft’s total mechanical energy is the sum of:
Potential Energy (Altitude) + Kinetic Energy (Airspeed)
An airplane in flight is an “open” energy system – This means two things:
The airplane can gain energy through thrust and lose energy through aerodynamic drag, and
Energy can be added or removed from the total energy and stored as airspeed or altitude
Energy Balance & Control
Energy management involves balancing thrust (T) & drag (D)
If T – D > 0 (T > D)      Total energy increases & can be applied to airspeed or altitude
If T – D < 0 (T < D)      Total energy decreases resulting in a descent or deceleration
If T – D = 0 (T = D)      Energy is constant – any changes in airspeed/altitude comes from trading one for the other
Energy Balance Equation (pictured below)
The left side of the equation represents the airplane’s total energy flow (Thrust & Drag)
The right side reflects the matching changes to energy storage (Altitude & Airspeed)
Any change in total energy due to thrust and drag is matched by a corresponding change in altitude or airspeed, ensuring energy conservation
Both sides of the equation are always balanced regardless of phase of flight
Pilot Control of Energy
Energy is controlled by changing the Pitch (elevator) & Power (throttle)
Throttle: Regulates energy by increasing or decreasing thrust
For simplicity’s sake, changes in total energy are normally initiated by changing thrust (not drag)
When the throttle setting makes thrust > drag, total energy increases and vice versa
With the desired path-speed profile established, the throttle is set to match the total energy needed by the vertical flight path + airspeed
Throttle is the total energy controller (left side of the energy balance equation)
Elevator: Adjusts the distribution of energy between altitude & airspeed
Allocates changes in total energy between the vertical flight path & airspeed by adjusting pitch attitude
With the desired path-speed profile established, the elevator sets pitch to maintain the desired distribution of total energy between the vertical flight path & airspeed
Elevator is the energy distribution controller (right side of the energy balance equation)
Reservoir Analogy (picture, right)
Throttle controls the valve regulating net energy flow
Elevator controls the valve regulating energy distribution in/out of the altitude & airspeed reservoirs
Advanced Elevator Concepts
Front Side of the Power Curve (top picture)
High speed/low AOA - Points 1 & A (no excess power)
Pulling back on the yoke causes a brief energy exchange climb that reduces airspeed (from 1 to 2)
Reduced speed = reduced drag (T – D > 0)
With excess power (B), the plane can climb at a constant airspeed or turn in level flight
Back Side of the Power Curve (top picture)
Low speed/high AOA - Points 3 & C (no excess power)
Pushing forward on the yoke causes a brief energy exchange descent that increases airspeed (from 3 to 2)
Increased speed = reduced drag (T – D > 0)
With excess power (B) the plane can climb at a constant airspeed or turn in level flight
Elevator’s Role in Increasing Drag (bottom pic)
In turns, the elevator can directly increase “D” in T - D
In a level turn, pulling back on the yoke increases AOA & load factor which increases drag & power required
Total energy is reduced faster than using throttle alone
Throttle & Elevator must be coordinated for a stable flight profile
The throttle & elevator are energy state controls (neither one controls altitude or speed independently)
To control altitude & airspeed, the pilot coordinates pitch & power to manage the plane’s energy state
Pitch + Power controls Energy State
3 Rules of Energy Control (for proper throttle-elevator coordination)
Increase Total Energy: Increase throttle (T > D) & pitch to distribute energy between altitude & speed
Climbing while maintaining speed      Pitch up just enough to maintain airspeed
Accelerating while maintaining altitude      Gradually pitch down just enough to maintain altitude
Decrease Total Energy: Reduce throttle (T < D) & pitch to distribute energy lost between altitude & speed
Descending while maintaining speed      Pitch down just enough to maintain airspeed
Accelerating while maintaining altitude      Gradually pitch up just enough to maintain path
Exchange Energy (without changing total energy): Pitch to exchange energy between altitude & airspeed
To trade speed for altitude      Pitch up
To trade altitude for speed      Pitch down
In all 3 situations, reaching the new energy state, adjust pitch & throttle to maintain the new speed-path profile
Energy Management Errors & Risks (2 Major Risks)
Unintended Altitude-Airspeed Deviations      Energy Errors
Total Energy Errors: Too much or too little energy (blue & red boxes)
Altitude & airspeed deviate in the same direction
Low & slow or high & fast
Corrected by increasing or decreasing energy with the throttle (bottom matrix)
Distribution Errors: Correct energy but wrong distribution (green boxes)
Altitude & airspeed deviate in opposite directions
High & slow or low & fast
Corrected by exchanging altitude & airspeed with the elevator (bottom matrix)
Distribution + Total Energy Errors
Throttle & elevator are used together
Example
Below glidepath on final approach
Solution to the problem depends on the situation
Reference diagram (below)
Vertical axis is altitude
Horizontal is airspeed
Airplane is low, but crosscheck airspeed
Low & Slow: B in diagram & 3 in matrices
Low & Fast: D in diagram & 9 in matrices
Low & On-speed: C in diagram & 6 in matrices
Unintentional, Irreversible Deceleration and/or Sink Rate
Unrecoverable depletion of energy
Due to loss of airspeed and/or energy + insufficient power available
Remember excess power is required to climb
Failure to recover above a certain altitude results in hitting the ground regardless of what the pilot does
Example (& the power curve – depicted right)
High altitude, hot day departure toward terrain
Approaching terrain, climb rate is not as expected
Pilot gradually pitches up, reducing speed
Airplane climbing at Speed 1/Point A
Slows to speed 2 – power available decreasing
The plane stops climbing (Point B)
Power available = power required
Stall horn (Point C)
Slower than Point B, power required is greater than power available
And the power required continues to increase
Irreversible rate of energy loss
Recovery: Must lower the nose and gain speed (VX) at the expense of altitude &/or turn around
Other Examples
Unstable/slow approach, high-drag go-around, steep turns in the pattern
Unrecoverable sink rates are also a threat at high speeds where excess power is 0 or negative
Ex: Poor steep turn leading to a high-speed steep spiral, high speed dives near the ground
Takeaways
Energy management is essential for all maneuvers, vertical flightpath and airspeed profiles, and is critical for safety – mismanagement is often hazardous
Throttle controls total energy & elevator manages its distribution between altitude & airspeed
Anticipate, recognize, & correct energy errors to avoid dangerous altitude or speed deviations

paragraphs.text: XV.B. Flight Review

References: Currency Requirements and Guidance for the Flight Review & IPC (AC 61-98), FAR 61.56 – Flight Review, Certificate: Pilots & Flight/Ground Instructors (AC 61-65), WINGS – Pilot Proficiency Programs (AC 61-91)
Purpose
A routine evaluation of a pilot’s ability to conduct safe flight
Not a test or checkride, rather a training event in which proficiency is evaluated
Role of the Instructor
Provide an evaluation, however instruction is also encouraged (they should leave a better pilot)
As long as deficiencies are corrected, providing instruction does not prevent a successful review
Flight Review Requirements – Minimum of 1 hour ground and 1 hour flight training, covering:
Current operating/flight rules (part 61/91)
Maneuvers/procedures that, at the discretion of the CFI, demonstrate safe operation
Aircraft –Must be accomplished in an aircraft for which the pilot (and CFI) is rated (FAR 61.56(c)(1))
If a pilot holds multiple ratings, a flight review in any one counts for all
Exceptions to the Flight Review – Within the last 24 months:
61.56(d) – Passed a practical test as described in the FAR
61.56(e) – Completed one or more phases of WINGS (more info: AC 61-91)
61.56(f) – Completed recent experience requirements (61.197) or reinstated certificate (61.199(a)(1))
Only removes the 1 hour of ground training requirements
Planning the Flight Review
Tailor the Review to the Pilot’s Needs (talk to the pilot to create a plan)
Type of aircraft, and type of flying usually done by the pilot
Amount and recency of flight experience
Specific topics/weaknesses they would like to focus on or review
AC 61-98 Focus Areas
Pilot Deviation Avoidance
Review airspace types/ground operating procedures/best practices to avoid deviations
Automation Competency
Numerous accidents/incidents have been attributed to a lack of proficiency in automation
AOA Systems (Safety initiative aimed at reducing the GA accident rate/loss of control accidents)
If equipped with AOA indicator, evaluate proper use. If not, review AOA aerodynamic principles
Build the Plan Based on the Individual - See sample Topics/Maneuvers below
Agreement on the review
Review the plan with the pilot to reach an understanding of how the flight review will be conducted
Review the criteria for satisfactory completion of the flight review (ex. ACS standards)
Post Flight Review
Debrief the pilot
Satisfactory or not, provide a comprehensive analysis of performance, including ways to improve
If unsatisfactory, log the flight as dual instruction given, not as a failure (not a checkride)
Offer a practical course of action to regain proficiency
Endorsement

paragraphs.text: XV.D. Common Carriage
References:
FAA Order 8900.1. Volume 2, Chapter 2, Section 2
AC 120-12A: Private vs Common Carriage
NBAA Certification of Commercial Aircraft Operations – Which Rules Apply?
This is a basic overview of common vs private carriage, certificates, and the like. For considerably more detail, use the reference links above, and additional information here:
How to Become a Certificated Air Carrier
FAR Part 119 – Certification: Air Carriers and Commercial Operators
FAR 61.133: Privileges & Limitations
Privileges – A person holding a commercial pilot certificate may act as PIC of an aircraft:
Carrying persons or property for compensation or hire
For compensation or hire
In both cases, the pilot must be qualified for the type of operation
Limitations
Commercial certificate without an instrument rating in the same category and class
Carriage of passengers for hire on flights more than 50 nautical miles or at night is prohibited
Limitation is lifted with an instrument rating in the same category and class
These privileges allow the pilot to act as PIC (i.e., someone can hire you to fly their plane)
Commercial certificate does not allow you to operate as an air carrier or commercial operator
The type of operation you’re hired to fly for will dictate the applicable FARs and governing regulations that they (and therefore you, as the pilot) operate under
The operation must decide whether they fall under common carriage or private carriage and drill down from there
Also applies if you’d like to start your own business as an air carrier or commercial operator
What is Common Carriage & Private Carriage?
Common Carriage and Private Carriage are common law terms
The Federal Aviation Act of 1958 uses the term “common carriage” but does not define it
AC 120-12 provides guidelines to define common carriage and its opposite, private carriage
Common Carriage
A carrier becomes a common carrier when it “holds itself out” to the public (or a segment of the public) as willing to provide transportation to any person who wants it
Holding Out
Makes a person a common carrier
Can be done in many ways, does not matter how it’s done
Examples
Signs and advertising are most direct means of holding out
Actions of agents or salesman who obtain passengers from the general public
A reputation to serve all (even without advertising)
4 Elements Defining a Common Carrier
A holding out of a willingness to
Transport persons or property
From place to place
For compensation
As a pilot with a commercial certificate, you cannot “hold out”
Illegal without the proper Part 119 certificates (more below)
Private Carriage
Carriage for hire which does not involve “holding out”
Carriage for one or several select customers, generally on a long-term basis
Too many contracts = willingness to make a contract with anybody (common carriage)
Governing Regulations
Once you’ve decided whether the operation falls under common carriage or private carriage, the next step is to decide what FAR regulations it falls under
Common carriage operations are required to be conducted under FAR Part 121, or Part 135 (depending on the type of aircraft, seating configuration, and payload capacity)
An operational certificate is required (issued under Part 119)
Two basic types of Air Operator Certificates:
Air Carrier Certificate: Issued for interstate, foreign, or overseas transportation, or to carry mail
Operating Certificate: Intrastate common carriage operations
Private carriage, on the other hand, is conducted under Part 125, Part 135 (again, depending on the type of aircraft, seating configuration, and payload capacity), or Part 91 Subpart D
Most private carriage also requires an operating certificate (exceptions for Part 91)
If they both require operating certificates, then what’s the difference?
Regulations and limitations – Generally, private carriage is less regulated than common carriage
Ex. Part 121 pilots rest rules
Kind of Operation
NOTE: This is getting into extra, possible overly confusing information. Unless the learner is considering starting their own operation it may not be necessary
The final step is to decide the kind of operation
Part 121
Domestic: Between two points inside the contiguous 48 states
Flag: Between a point outside of contiguous 48 states to a point inside the contiguous 48
Supplemental: Cargo, charter, departure location/times are negotiated with customer (vs scheduled)
Part 135
Commuter: Scheduled time and locations with at least 5 round trip flights per week
On-Demand: Departure time and location and arrival location are negotiated with the customer
FAA Order 8900.1. Volume 2, Chapter 2, Section 2
Table 2-4 looks at the Operating Certificate, Seating/Payload, 14 CFR Operating Part, & Kind of Op.
FAR 119.1(e) Exceptions
Operations for compensation/hire that don’t require an air carrier or commercial operator certificate
Student instruction
Nonstop commercial air tours (a lot more detail to this in the FAR)
Ferry or training flight
Aerial work (crop dusting, seeding, spraying, banner towering, aerial photography, and more)
Parachute operations within 25 statute miles of the airport
Part 375 operations (foreign civil aircraft in the US)
Emergency mail service
Operations under part 91.321 (carriage of candidates in elections)
Confused?
Discuss any proposed operation with the FAA
Early discussions can prevent a lot of pitfalls and potential illegal operations

Big Picture: As a commercial pilot you can be hired to fly for an operation but, other than the FAR 119.1(e) exceptions, you cannot hold out or offer your services without the proper FAA/FAR approval and certificate

paragraphs.text: XV.E. ADM, CRM & SRM
Introduction
How
Aeronautical Decision Making (ADM)
A systematic approach to the mental process used by aircraft pilots to consistently determine the best course of action in response to a given set of circumstances
Teaching pilots to make sound decisions is the key to preventing accidents
It is estimated that approximately 80% of all aviation accidents are a result of human factors
Steps for Good Decision Making
Identify personal attitudes hazardous to safety & learn behavior modification techniques
Learn how to recognize and cope with stress
Develop risk assessment skills
Use all resources
Evaluate effectiveness of one’s ADM skills
Risk Assessment & Management
4 Fundamental Principles of Risk Management
The goal of these principles is to proactively identify safety-related hazards & mitigate associated risks
Accept no Unnecessary Risk
Only accept the necessary risk
Flying inherently contains some risk, do not make a situation more dangerous than necessary
Make Risk Decisions at the Appropriate Level
In single pilot situations, the pilot makes decisions (not ATC, or passengers)
In other situations, it may be beneficial to “go up the ladder” for a decision
i.e., Talk to the chief pilot or experienced CFI about a potentially risky situation
Accept Risk When Benefits Outweigh the Costs
Analyze costs and benefits, make an informed decision
Integrate Risk Management into Planning at All Levels
Safety requires risk management planning in all stages of flight
Plan early and throughout to avoid unnecessary, amplified risk
Risk Management Process
Step 1: Identify the Hazard
A hazard is any real or potential condition that can cause degradation, injury, illness, death, damage to or loss of equipment or property
Step 2: Assess the Risk
Determine the level of risk associated with the identified hazards
Assess in terms of its likelihood (probability) and its severity (consequences)
Develop a method to tangibly measure risk (Risk Assessment Matrix, below)
Step 3: Mitigate the Risk
Look into ways to reduce, mitigate, or eliminate the risk
All risks have 2 components: Probability of occurrence & Severity of the hazard
Try to reduce or eliminate at least one component
Use the Cost/Benefit analysis to decide if it is worth accepting the risk
Level of Risk
The level of risk posed by a given hazard is measured in terms of:
Severity (extent of possible loss)
Likelihood (probability that a hazard will cause a loss)
Assessing Risk
Pilots must differentiate in advance between a low risk ﬂight and a high-risk ﬂight
Establish a review process and develop strategies to minimize risk on the high and low risk flights
The Risk Matrix is a helpful risk assessment model
Assesses the likelihood of an event occurring and the consequences of that event
Likelihood (probability of occurrence): Probable, Occasional, Remote, Improbable
i.e., Likelihood of a pilot flying MVFR to encounter IFR conditions
Severity: Catastrophic, Critical, Marginal, Negligible
i.e., How severe the consequences could be if the pilot is not IFR rated
High Probability/Severity is bad and vice versa
Mitigating Risk
After determining the level of risk, the pilot needs to reduce the risk
Analyze options that can reduce unnecessary risk
Ex. Cancel/delay flight, bring CFI or more experienced pilot, etc.
By effectively mitigating known risks to acceptable levels, pilots can complete their flights safely or ensure alternate options are selected for the occasions when the flight cannot be accomplished
PAVE Checklist
A tool to assess & manage risk: Risk is divided into 4 categories – Assess the situation by category and decide whether the risks can be managed safely. If not, cancel the flight
Pilot: Am I ready? (IMSAFE Checklist, proficiency, recency, currency, etc.)
Aircraft: Is the aircraft appropriate for the trip?
Maintenance, Landing Distance, Performance Capabilities, Equipment, Fuel load, Altitude, etc.
EnVironment: Weather, Terrain, Airports, Airspace, Day/Night, etc.
External Pressures: Influences outside of the flight that create pressure to complete the flight
Very important as this is the one risk factor that can cause a pilot to ignore all other risk factors
Follow your own personal operating procedures (don’t bend the rules for anyone), plan for delays, and manage passenger’s expectations to reduce external pressure
Single Pilot Resource Management / Crew Resource Management (Use all Resources)
What is it?
How to gather information, analyze it, and make decisions
Application of team management concepts in the flight deck environment
Includes all groups routinely working with the flight crew who are involved in decisions required to operate a flight safely
Ex. Pilots, dispatchers, cabin crew, maintenance, ATC
Pilots of small and large aircraft must make effective us of all available resources
Use of Resources
Use all available resources - Think outside the box
Internal Resources
Found in the flight deck during flight
Equipment, systems, charts, books, etc.
Ingenuity, knowledge, and skill
Other passengers (even if they are not pilots)
External Resources
ATC and flight service specialists
Traffic advisories, vectors, weather info, emergency assistance
Workload Management
Plan, prioritize, and sequence to prevent overload
Prepare for high workload situations
Don’t wait until you’re in the situation
i.e., prepare for the approach before it begins
Be able to recognize high workloads
Faster paced work along with divided attention
Stay ahead as much as possible to prevent high workloads
Manage tasks in order of importance when behind
5 P’s Check
Used to evaluate the situation at key points during the ﬂight, or when an emergency arises - Based on the idea that the pilot has 5 variables that impact the environment and lead to a decision
Procedure
At least 5 times, review the 5 P’s and make a decision based on the current situation
Preflight – Pre-takeoff – Hourly or Midpoint of flight – Pre-descent – FAF or entering the pattern
Very helpful part of Single Pilot Resource Management (SRM)
5 P’s
Plan
The mission. It contains planning, weather, route, fuel, publication currency, etc.
The plan is always changing (weather changes, delays, restrictions, etc.), adjust with it
Plane
Condition, abilities (performance, automation, database, etc.), equipment, systems, etc.
Pilot
IMSAFE
Allows the pilot to recognize and review his/her physiological situation
Passengers
Passenger’s desires can have an influence on decision making and risk management
Ensure passengers are involved in decision making process
Ensure they understand risk involved in situations
i.e., IFR approach below minimums or takeoff with IFR below landing minimums
Understand what passengers want to do - They may be more risk averse than you
Programming
Plan when and where programming should & should not be accomplished
Familiarity with the equipment, route, local air trafﬁc control environment, etc. should drive when, where, how the automation is programmed and used
Consider pilot capabilities in relation to programming
Decision Making Process
DECIDE Model (pictured below)
Detect, Estimate, Choose, Identify, Do, Evaluate
Analytical Models
Examples include DECIDE model and 5 Ps
Good decisions result when pilots gather all information, review it, analyze the options, rate the options, select a course of action, and evaluate the course of action for correctness
This level of analysis is not always possible
Automatic or Naturalized Decision Making
Reflexive type of decision making anchored in training and experience
In an emergency, a pilot may not survive if they apply analytical models to every decision
Automatic or Naturalized Process
Experts faced with a task loaded with uncertainty first assess if the situation looks familiar
Rather than comparing pros and cons of different approaches (analytical model), they imagine how one or a few courses of action will play out and take the first workable option they find
May not be the best of all possible choices, but it often works remarkably well
Experienced based actions trigger response to specific situations
Improves with training and experience
Operational Pitfalls
Pitfalls/behavioral traps also come with experience
As a rule, more experienced pilots try to complete flights as planned, please passengers, meet schedules
Can have an adverse effect on safety and contribute to unrealistic assessment of skills
Tendencies must be eliminated
Evaluation
Review and debrief every flight
What went well?
What could have gone better?
What will I (or we) do next time?
Areas to Consider in the Evaluation
Planning & Decision Making
Leadership Effectiveness
Situational Awareness
Communication
Monitor/Cross-Check
Workload Management
Automation Management

XV.E. ADM, CRM & SRM
Introduction
How
Aeronautical Decision Making (ADM)
A systematic approach to the mental process used by aircraft pilots to consistently determine the best course of action in response to a given set of circumstances
Teaching pilots to make sound decisions is the key to preventing accidents
It is estimated that approximately 80% of all aviation accidents are a result of human factors
Steps for Good Decision Making
Identify personal attitudes hazardous to safety & learn behavior modification techniques
Learn how to recognize and cope with stress
Develop risk assessment skills
Use all resources
Evaluate effectiveness of one’s ADM skills
Risk Assessment & Management
4 Fundamental Principles of Risk Management
The goal of these principles is to proactively identify safety-related hazards & mitigate associated risks
Accept no Unnecessary Risk
Only accept the necessary risk
Flying inherently contains some risk, do not make a situation more dangerous than necessary
Make Risk Decisions at the Appropriate Level
In single pilot situations, the pilot makes decisions (not ATC, or passengers)
In other situations, it may be beneficial to “go up the ladder” for a decision
i.e., Talk to the chief pilot or experienced CFI about a potentially risky situation
Accept Risk When Benefits Outweigh the Costs
Analyze costs and benefits, make an informed decision
Integrate Risk Management into Planning at All Levels
Safety requires risk management planning in all stages of flight
Plan early and throughout to avoid unnecessary, amplified risk
Risk Management Process
Step 1: Identify the Hazard
A hazard is any real or potential condition that can cause degradation, injury, illness, death, damage to or loss of equipment or property
Step 2: Assess the Risk
Determine the level of risk associated with the identified hazards
Assess in terms of its likelihood (probability) and its severity (consequences)
Develop a method to tangibly measure risk (Risk Assessment Matrix, below)
Step 3: Mitigate the Risk
Look into ways to reduce, mitigate, or eliminate the risk
All risks have 2 components: Probability of occurrence & Severity of the hazard
Try to reduce or eliminate at least one component
Use the Cost/Benefit analysis to decide if it is worth accepting the risk

The level of risk posed by a given hazard is measured in terms of:
Severity (extent of possible loss)
Likelihood (probability that a hazard will cause a loss)

Establish a review process and develop strategies to minimize risk on the high and low risk flights

paragraphs.text: A. Energy Management
Airplane Flying Handbook Ch. 4
What is it & Why is it Important?
What: Process of controlling altitude and airspeed to maintain safe and efficient flight
Why: Critical to flight safety and essential for basic & advanced airmanship skills
Prevents loss of control in flight (LOC-I), controlled flight into terrain (CFIT), approach & landing accidents
Essential for maintaining vertical flight paths & airspeed profiles and transitioning between flight profiles
Ex. Final approach, constant airspeed climb, or leveling off from a descent
The Airplane as an Energy System
An aircraft’s total mechanical energy is the sum of:
Potential Energy (Altitude) + Kinetic Energy (Airspeed)
An airplane in flight is an “open” energy system – This means two things:
The airplane can gain energy through thrust and lose energy through aerodynamic drag, and
Energy can be added or removed from the total energy and stored as airspeed or altitude
Energy Balance & Control
Energy management involves balancing thrust (T) & drag (D)
If T – D > 0 (T > D)      Total energy increases & can be applied to airspeed or altitude
If T – D < 0 (T < D)      Total energy decreases resulting in a descent or deceleration
If T – D = 0 (T = D)      Energy is constant – any changes in airspeed/altitude come from trading one for the other
Energy Balance Equation (pictured below)
The left side of the equation represents the airplane’s total energy flow (Thrust & Drag)
The right side reflects the matching changes to energy storage (Altitude & Airspeed)
Any change in total energy due to thrust and drag is matched by a corresponding change in altitude or airspeed, ensuring energy conservation
Both sides of the equation are always balanced regardless of phase of flight
Pilot Control of Energy
Energy is controlled by changing the Pitch (elevator) & Power (throttle)
Throttle: Regulates energy by increasing or decreasing thrust
For simplicity’s sake, changes in total energy are normally initiated by changing thrust (not drag)
When the throttle setting makes thrust > drag, total energy increases and vice versa
With the desired path-speed profile established, the throttle is set to match the total energy needed by the vertical flight path + airspeed
Throttle is the total energy controller (left side of the energy balance equation)
Elevator: Adjusts the distribution of energy between altitude & airspeed
Allocates changes in total energy between the vertical flight path & airspeed by adjusting pitch attitude
With the desired path-speed profile established, the elevator sets pitch to maintain the desired distribution of total energy between the vertical flight path & airspeed
Elevator is the energy distribution controller (right side of the energy balance equation)
Reservoir Analogy (top picture)
Throttle controls the valve regulating net energy flow
Elevator controls the valve regulating energy distribution in/out of the altitude & airspeed reservoirs
Advanced Elevator Concepts
Front Side of the Power Curve (middle picture)
High speed/low AOA - Points 1 & A (no excess power)
Pulling back on the yoke causes a brief energy exchange climb that reduces airspeed (from 1 to 2)
Reduced speed = reduced drag (T – D > 0)
With excess power (B), the plane can climb at a constant airspeed or turn in level flight
Back Side of the Power Curve (middle picture)
Low speed/high AOA - Points 3 & C (no excess power)
Pushing forward on the yoke causes a brief energy exchange descent that increases airspeed (from 3 to 2)
Increased speed = reduced drag (T – D > 0)
With excess power (B) the plane can climb at a constant airspeed or turn in level flight
Elevator’s Role in Increasing Drag (bottom picture)
In turns, the elevator can directly increase “D” in T - D
In a level turn, pulling back on the yoke increases AOA & load factor which increases drag & power required
Total energy is reduced faster than using throttle alone
Throttle & Elevator must be coordinated for a stable flight profile
The throttle & elevator are energy state controls (neither one controls altitude or airspeed independently)
To control altitude & airspeed, the pilot coordinates pitch & power to manage the plane’s energy state
Pitch + Power controls Energy State
3 Rules of Energy Control (for proper throttle-elevator coordination)
To increase total energy: Increase throttle (so T > D) & pitch to distribute energy between altitude & airspeed
Climbing while maintaining speed      Pitch up just enough to maintain airspeed
Accelerating while maintaining altitude      Gradually pitch down just enough to maintain altitude
To decrease total energy: Reduce throttle (T < D) & pitch to distribute energy lost between altitude & airspeed
Descending while maintaining speed      Pitch down just enough to maintain airspeed
Accelerating while maintaining altitude      Gradually pitch up just enough to maintain path
To exchange energy (without changing total energy): Pitch to exchange energy between altitude & airspeed
To trade speed for altitude      Pitch up
To trade altitude for speed      Pitch down
In all 3 situations, reaching the new energy state, adjust pitch & throttle to maintain the new speed-path profile
Energy Management Errors & Risks (2 Major Risks)
Unintended Altitude-Airspeed Deviations      Energy Errors
Total Energy Errors: Too much or too little energy (blue & red boxes)
Altitude & airspeed deviate in the same direction
Low & slow or high & fast
Corrected by increasing or decreasing energy with the throttle (middle altitude/airspeed matrix)
Distribution Errors: Correct energy but incorrect distribution (green boxes)
Altitude & airspeed deviate in opposite directions
High & slow or low & fast
Corrected by exchanging altitude & airspeed with the elevator (middle altitude/airspeed matrix)
Distribution + Total Energy Errors
Throttle & elevator are used together
Example
Below glidepath on final approach
Solution to the problem depends on the situation
Reference diagram, bottom picture on right
Vertical axis is altitude
Horizontal axis is airspeed
Airplane is low, but crosscheck airspeed
Low & Slow: B in diagram & 3 in matrices
Low & Fast: D in diagram & 9 in matrices
Low & On-speed: C in diagram & 6 in matrices
Unintentional, irreversible deceleration and/or sink rate
Unrecoverable depletion of energy
Due to loss of airspeed and/or energy + insufficient power available
Remember excess power is required to climb
Failure to recover above a certain altitude results in hitting the ground regardless of what the pilot does
Example (& the power curve – depicted below)
High altitude, hot day departure toward terrain
Approaching terrain, climb rate is not as expected
Pilot gradually pitches up, reducing airspeed
Airplane climbing at Speed 1/Point A
Slows to speed 2 – power available decreasing
The plane stops climbing (Point B)
Power available = power required
Stall horn (Point C)
Slower than Point B, power required is > power available
And the power required continues to increase
Irreversible rate of energy loss
Recovery: Must lower the nose and gain speed (VX) at the expense of altitude &/or turn around
Other Examples
Unstable/slow approach, high-drag go-around, steep turns in the pattern
Unrecoverable sink rates are also a threat at high speeds where excess power is 0 or negative
Ex: Poor steep turn leading to a high-speed steep spiral, high speed dives too close to the ground
Takeaways
Energy management is essential for all maneuvers, desired vertical flightpath and airspeed profiles, and is critical for safety – mismanagement is often hazardous
Throttle controls total energy & elevator manages its distribution between altitude & airspeed
Pilots must anticipate, recognize, & correct energy errors to avoid dangerous altitude or speed deviations
Conclusion:
Brief review of the main points

Purpose
A routine evaluation of a pilot’s ability to conduct safe flight
Not a test or checkride, rather a training event in which proficiency is evaluated
Role of the Instructor
Provide an evaluation, however instruction is also encouraged (they should leave a better pilot)
As long as deficiencies are corrected, providing instruction does not prevent a successful review
Flight Review Requirements – Minimum of 1 hour ground and 1 hour flight training, covering:
Current operating/flight rules (part 61/91)
Maneuvers/procedures that, at the discretion of the CFI, demonstrate safe operation
Aircraft –Must be accomplished in an aircraft for which the pilot (and CFI) is rated (FAR 61.56(c)(1))
If a pilot holds multiple ratings, a flight review in any one counts for all
Exceptions to the Flight Review – Within the last 24 months:
61.56(d) – Passed a practical test as described in the FAR
61.56(e) – Completed one or more phases of WINGS (more info: AC 61-91)
61.56(f) – Completed recent experience requirements (61.197) or reinstated certificate (61.199(a)(1))
Only removes the 1 hour of ground training requirements
Planning the Flight Review
Tailor the Review to the Pilot’s Needs (talk to the pilot to create a plan)

paragraphs.text: D. Common Carriage
References:
FAA Order 8900.1. Volume 2, Chapter 2, Section 2
AC 120-12A: Private vs Common Carriage
NBAA Certification of Commercial Aircraft Operations – Which Rules Apply?
This is a basic overview of common vs private carriage, certificates, and the like. For considerably more detail, use the reference links above, and additional information here:
How to Become a Certificated Air Carrier
FAR Part 119 – Certification: Air Carriers and Commercial Operators
FAR 61.133: Privileges and Limitations
Privileges – A person holding a commercial pilot certificate may act as PIC of an aircraft:
Carrying persons or property for compensation or hire
For compensation or hire
In both cases, the pilot must be qualified for the type of operation
Limitations
Commercial certificate without an instrument rating in the same category and class
Carriage of passengers for hire on cross-country flights more than 50 nautical miles at night is prohibited
Limitations is lifted with an instrument rating in the same category and class
These privileges allow the pilot to act as PIC – i.e., someone can hire you to fly their plane
Commercial certificate does not allow you to operate as an air carrier or commercial operator
The type of operation you’re hired to fly for will dictate the applicable FARs and governing regulations that they (and therefore you, as the pilot) operate under
The operation has to decide whether they fall under common carriage or private carriage and drill down from there
Also applies if you’d like to start you own business as an air carrier or commercial operator
What is Common Carriage & Private Carriage?
Common Carriage and Private Carriage are common law terms
The Federal Aviation Act of 1958 uses the term “common carriage” but does not define it
AC 120-12 provides guidelines to define common carriage and its opposite, private carriage
Common Carriage
A carrier becomes a common carrier when it “holds itself out” to the public (or a segment of the public) as willing to provide transportation to any person who wants it
Holding Out
Makes a person a common carrier
Can be done in many ways, does not matter how it’s done
Examples
Signs and advertising are most direct means of holding out
Actions of agents or salesman who obtain passengers from the general public
A reputation to serve all (even without advertising)
4 elements defining a common carrier
A holding out of a willingness to
Transport persons or property
From place to place
For compensation
As a pilot with a commercial certificate, you cannot “hold out”
Illegal without the proper Part 119 certificates (more below)
Private Carriage
Carriage for hire which does not involve “holding out”
Carriage for one or several select customers, generally on a long-term basis
Too many contracts = willingness to make a contract with anybody (common carriage)
Governing Regulations
Once you’ve decided whether the operation falls under common carriage or private carriage, the next step is to decide what FAR regulations it falls under
Common carriage operations are required to be conducted under FAR Part 121, or Part 135 (depending on the type of aircraft, seating configuration, and payload capacity)
An operational certificate is required (issued under Part 119)
Two basic types of Air Operator Certificates:
Air Carrier Certificate: Issued for interstate, foreign, or overseas transportation, or to carry mail
Operating Certificate: Intrastate common carriage operations
Private carriage, on the other hand, is conducted under Part 125, Part 135 (again, depending on the type of aircraft, seating configuration, and payload capacity), or Part 91 Subpart D
Most private carriage also requires an operating certificate (exceptions for Part 91)
If they both require operating certificates, then what’s the difference?
Regulations and limitations
Generally, private carriage is less regulated than common carriage
Ex. Part 121 pilots rest rules
Kind of Operation
Note: this is getting into extra, possible overly confusing information. Unless the learner is considering starting their own operation it may not be necessary
The final step is to decide the kind of operation
Part 121
Domestic: Between two points inside the contiguous 48 states
Flag: Between a point outside of contiguous 48 states to a point inside the contiguous 48
Supplemental: Cargo, charter, departure location/times are negotiated with customer (vs scheduled)
Part 135
Commuter: Scheduled time and locations with at least 5 round trip flights per week
On-demand: Departure time and location and arrival location are negotiated with the customer
FAA Order 8900.1. Volume 2, Chapter 2, Section 2
Table 2-4 looks at the Operating Certificate, Seating/Payload, 14 CFR Operating Part, & Kind of Op.
FAR 119.1(e) Exceptions
Operations for compensation or hire that do not require an air carrier or commercial operator certificate
Student instruction
Nonstop commercial air tours (a lot more detail to this in the FAR)
Ferry or training flight
Aerial work (crop dusting, seeding, spraying, banner towering, aerial photography, and more)
Parachute operations within 25 statute miles of the airport
Part 375 operations (foreign civil aircraft in the US)
Emergency mail service
Operations under part 91.321 (carriage of candidates in elections)
Confused?
Discuss any proposed operation with the FAA
Early discussions can prevent a lot of pitfalls and potential illegal operations

As a commercial pilot you can be hired to fly for an operation but, other than the FAR 119.1(e) exceptions, you cannot hold out or offer your services without the proper FAA/FAR approval and certificate

paragraphs.text: E. ADM, CRM & SRM
References: Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25)
Instructor Notes:
Introduction:
Attention
Interesting fact or attention-grabbing story
Overview
Review Objectives and Elements/Key ideas
What
A systematic approach to the mental process used by aircraft pilots to consistently determine the best course of action in response to a given set of circumstances
Why
Despite all the changes in technology to improve flight safety, one factor remains the same: the human factor which leads to errors.
How:
Aeronautical Decision Making (ADM)
A systematic approach to the mental process used by aircraft pilots to consistently determine the best course of action in response to a given set of circumstances
Teaching pilots to make sound decisions is the key to preventing accidents
It is estimated that approximately 80% of all aviation accidents are a result of human factors
Steps for Good Decision Making
Identify personal attitudes hazardous to safety & learn behavior modification techniques
Learn how to recognize and cope with stress
Develop risk assessment skills
Use all resources
Evaluate effectiveness of one’s ADM skills
Risk Assessment & Management
4 Fundamental Principles of Risk Management
Goal of these principles is to proactively identify safety-related hazards and mitigate associated risks
Accept no Unnecessary Risk
Only accept the necessary risk
Flying is impossible without risk, do not make a situation more dangerous than necessary
Make Risk Decisions at the Appropriate Level
In single pilot situations, the pilot makes decisions (not ATC, or passengers)
In other situations, it may be beneficial to “go up the ladder” for a decision
i.e., Talk to the chief pilot or experienced CFI about a potentially risky situation
Accept Risk When Benefits Outweigh the Costs
Analyze costs and benefits, make an informed decision
Integrate Risk Management into Planning at All Levels
Safety requires risk management planning in all stages of flight
Plan early and throughout to avoid unnecessary, amplified risk
Risk Management Process
Step 1: Identify the Hazard
A hazard is any real or potential condition that can cause degradation, injury, illness, death, damage to or loss of equipment or property
Step 2: Assess the Risk
Determine the level of risk associated with the identified hazards
Assess in terms of its likelihood (probability) and its severity (consequences)
Develop a method to tangibly measure risk (Risk Assessment Matrix, below)
Step 3: Mitigate the Risk
Look into ways to reduce, mitigate, or eliminate the risk
All risks have 2 components: Probability of occurrence & Severity of the hazard
Try to reduce or eliminate at least one component
Use the Cost/Benefit analysis to decide if it is worth accepting the risk
Level of Risk
The level of risk posed by a given hazard is measured in terms of:
Severity (extent of possible loss)
Probability (likelihood that a hazard will cause a loss)
Assessing Risk
Pilots must differentiate in advance between a low risk ﬂight and a high-risk ﬂight
Establish a review process and develop strategies to minimize risk on the high and low risk flights
The Risk Matrix is a helpful risk assessment model
Assesses the likelihood of an event occurring and the consequences of that event
Likelihood (probability of occurrence): Probable, Occasional, Remote, Improbable
i.e., Likelihood of a pilot flying MVFR to encounter IFR conditions
Severity: Catastrophic, Critical, Marginal, Negligible
i.e., How severe the consequences could be if the pilot is not IFR rated
High Probability/Severity is bad and vice versa:
Mitigating Risk
After determining the level of risk, the pilot needs to reduce the risk
Analyze options that can reduce unnecessary risk
i.e., Cancel/delay flight, bring CFI or more experienced pilot, etc.
By effectively mitigating known risks to acceptable levels, pilots can complete their flights safely or ensure alternate options are selected for the occasions when the flight cannot be accomplished
PAVE Checklist
Another way to mitigate risk
The risks of flight are divided into 4 categories
Once the risks have been identified, decide whether the risk or combination or risks can be managed safely and successfully. If not, the flight should be cancelled
Pilot in Command: Am I ready? (IMSAFE Checklist, proficiency, recency, currency, etc.)
Aircraft: Is the aircraft appropriate for the trip?
Maintenance, Landing Distance, Performance Capabilities, Equipment, Fuel load, Altitude, etc.
EnVironment: Weather, Terrain, Airports, Airspace, Day/Night, etc.
External Pressures: Influences outside of the flight that create pressure to complete the flight, often at the expense of safety
This is the most important key to risk management because it is the one risk factor category that can cause a pilot to ignore all the other risk factors
Follow your own personal operating procedures (don’t bend the rules for anyone), plan for delays, and manage passenger’s expectations to reduce external pressure
Single Pilot Resource Management / Crew Resource Management (Use all Resources)
What is it?
How to gather information, analyze it, and make decisions
Application of team management concepts in the flight deck environment
Includes all groups routinely working with the flight crew who are involved in decisions required to operate a flight safely
Pilots, dispatchers, cabin crew, maintenance, ATC
Pilots of small and large aircraft must make effective us of all available resources
Use of Resources
Use all available resources,
Think outside the box
Internal Resources
Found in the flight deck during flight
Equipment, systems, charts, books, etc.
Ingenuity, knowledge, and skill
Other passengers (even if they are not pilots)
External Resources
ATC and flight service specialists
Traffic advisories, vectors, weather info, emergency assistance
Workload Management
Plan, prioritize, and sequence to prevent overload
Prepare for high workload situations
Don’t wait until you’re in the situation
i.e., prepare for the approach before it begins
Be able to recognize high workloads
Faster paced work along with divided attention
Stay ahead as much as possible to prevent high workloads
Manage tasks in order of importance when behind
5 P’s Check
Used to evaluate the pilot’s current situation at key decision points during the ﬂight, or when an emergency arises
This is a very helpful portion of Single Pilot Resource Management (SRM)

Based on the idea that the pilot has five variables that impact the environment and can cause the pilot to make a single critical decision, or several less critical decisions, that when added together can create a critical outcome
The process is simple; at least 5 times before/during the flight, review and consider the 5 P’s and make the appropriate decision required by the current situation
The decision points include preflight, pre-takeoff, hourly or at the midpoint of flight, pre-descent, and just prior to the final approach fix or entering the traffic pattern
The 5 P’s:
The Plan
The mission. It contains planning, weather, route, fuel, publication currency, etc.
The plan is always changing (weather changes, delays, restrictions, etc.), adjust with it
The Plane
Condition, abilities (performance, but also automation, database currency, etc.), equipment, systems, etc.
The Pilot
IMSAFE
Allows the pilot to recognize and review his/her physiological situation
The Passengers
Passenger’s desires can have an influence on decision making and risk management
Plan as much as possible
Ensure passengers are involved in decision making process
Ensure they understand risk involved in situations
i.e., IFR approach below minimums or takeoff with IFR below landing minimums
Understand what passengers want to do
They may be more risk averse than you
The Programming
Plan when and where programming approaches/route changes, and airport information gathering should be accomplished, as well as when it should not be accomplished
Pilot familiarity with the equipment, the route, the local air trafﬁc control environment, and personal capabilities should drive when, where, how the automation is programmed and used
Always consider pilot capabilities in relation to programming
Decision Making Process
DECIDE Model (pictured below)
Detect, Estimate, Choose, Identify, Do, Evaluate
Analytical Models
Examples include DECIDE model and 5 Ps
Good decisions result when pilots gather all information, review it, analyze the options, rate the options, select a course of action, and evaluate the course of action for correctness
This level of analysis is not always possible
Automatic or Naturalized Decision Making
Reflexive type of decision making anchored in training and experience
In an emergency, a pilot may not survive if they apply analytical models to every decision
Automatic or Naturalized Process
Experts faced with a task loaded with uncertainty first assess if the situation looks familiar
Rather than comparing pros and cons of different approaches (analytical model), they imagine how one or a few courses of action will play out and take the first workable option they find
May not be the best of all possible choices, but it often works remarkably well
Experienced based actions trigger response to specific situations
Improves with training and experience
Operational Pitfalls (pictured below)
Pitfalls/behavioral traps also come with experience
As a rule, more experienced pilots try to complete flights as planned, please passengers, meet schedules
Can have an adverse effect on safety and contribute to unrealistic assessment of skills
Tendencies must be eliminated
Evaluation
Review and debrief each flight
What went well?
What could have gone better?
What will I (or we) do next time?
Areas to Consider in the Evaluation
Planning & Decision Making
Leadership Effectiveness
Situational Awareness
Communication
Monitor/Cross-Check
Workload Management
Automation Management
Conclusion:
Brief review of the main points

E. ADM, CRM & SRM
References: Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25)
Instructor Notes:
Introduction:
Attention
Interesting fact or attention-grabbing story
Overview
Review Objectives and Elements/Key ideas
What
A systematic approach to the mental process used by aircraft pilots to consistently determine the best course of action in response to a given set of circumstances
Why
Despite all the changes in technology to improve flight safety, one factor remains the same: the human factor which leads to errors.
How:
Aeronautical Decision Making (ADM)
A systematic approach to the mental process used by aircraft pilots to consistently determine the best course of action in response to a given set of circumstances
Teaching pilots to make sound decisions is the key to preventing accidents
It is estimated that approximately 80% of all aviation accidents are a result of human factors
Steps for Good Decision Making
Identify personal attitudes hazardous to safety & learn behavior modification techniques
Learn how to recognize and cope with stress
Develop risk assessment skills
Use all resources
Evaluate effectiveness of one’s ADM skills
Risk Assessment & Management
4 Fundamental Principles of Risk Management
Goal of these principles is to proactively identify safety-related hazards and mitigate associated risks
Accept no Unnecessary Risk
Only accept the necessary risk
Flying is impossible without risk, do not make a situation more dangerous than necessary
Make Risk Decisions at the Appropriate Level
In single pilot situations, the pilot makes decisions (not ATC, or passengers)
In other situations, it may be beneficial to “go up the ladder” for a decision
i.e., Talk to the chief pilot or experienced CFI about a potentially risky situation
Accept Risk When Benefits Outweigh the Costs
Analyze costs and benefits, make an informed decision
Integrate Risk Management into Planning at All Levels
Safety requires risk management planning in all stages of flight
Plan early and throughout to avoid unnecessary, amplified risk
Risk Management Process
Step 1: Identify the Hazard
A hazard is any real or potential condition that can cause degradation, injury, illness, death, damage to or loss of equipment or property
Step 2: Assess the Risk
Determine the level of risk associated with the identified hazards
Assess in terms of its likelihood (probability) and its severity (consequences)
Develop a method to tangibly measure risk (Risk Assessment Matrix, below)
Step 3: Mitigate the Risk
Look into ways to reduce, mitigate, or eliminate the risk
All risks have 2 components: Probability of occurrence & Severity of the hazard
Try to reduce or eliminate at least one component
Use the Cost/Benefit analysis to decide if it is worth accepting the risk
Level of Risk
The level of risk posed by a given hazard is measured in terms of:
Severity (extent of possible loss)
Probability (likelihood that a hazard will cause a loss)
Assessing Risk
Pilots must differentiate in advance between a low risk ﬂight and a high-risk ﬂight
Establish a review process and develop strategies to minimize risk on the high and low risk flights
The Risk Matrix is a helpful risk assessment model
Assesses the likelihood of an event occurring and the consequences of that event
Likelihood (probability of occurrence): Probable, Occasional, Remote, Improbable
i.e., Likelihood of a pilot flying MVFR to encounter IFR conditions
Severity: Catastrophic, Critical, Marginal, Negligible
i.e., How severe the consequences could be if the pilot is not IFR rated
High Probability/Severity is bad and vice versa:
Mitigating Risk
After determining the level of risk, the pilot needs to reduce the risk
Analyze options that can reduce unnecessary risk
i.e., Cancel/delay flight, bring CFI or more experienced pilot, etc.
By effectively mitigating known risks to acceptable levels, pilots can complete their flights safely or ensure alternate options are selected for the occasions when the flight cannot be accomplished
PAVE Checklist
Another way to mitigate risk
The risks of flight are divided into 4 categories
Once the risks have been identified, decide whether the risk or combination or risks can be managed safely and successfully. If not, the flight should be cancelled
Pilot in Command: Am I ready? (IMSAFE Checklist, proficiency, recency, currency, etc.)
Aircraft: Is the aircraft appropriate for the trip?
Maintenance, Landing Distance, Performance Capabilities, Equipment, Fuel load, Altitude, etc.
EnVironment: Weather, Terrain, Airports, Airspace, Day/Night, etc.
External Pressures: Influences outside of the flight that create pressure to complete the flight, often at the expense of safety
This is the most important key to risk management because it is the one risk factor category that can cause a pilot to ignore all the other risk factors
Follow your own personal operating procedures (don’t bend the rules for anyone), plan for delays, and manage passenger’s expectations to reduce external pressure
Single Pilot Resource Management / Crew Resource Management (Use all Resources)
What is it?
How to gather information, analyze it, and make decisions
Application of team management concepts in the flight deck environment
Includes all groups routinely working with the flight crew who are involved in decisions required to operate a flight safely
Pilots, dispatchers, cabin crew, maintenance, ATC
Pilots of small and large aircraft must make effective us of all available resources
Use of Resources
Use all available resources,
Think outside the box
Internal Resources
Found in the flight deck during flight
Equipment, systems, charts, books, etc.
Ingenuity, knowledge, and skill
Other passengers (even if they are not pilots)
External Resources
ATC and flight service specialists
Traffic advisories, vectors, weather info, emergency assistance
Workload Management
Plan, prioritize, and sequence to prevent overload
Prepare for high workload situations
Don’t wait until you’re in the situation
i.e., prepare for the approach before it begins
Be able to recognize high workloads
Faster paced work along with divided attention
Stay ahead as much as possible to prevent high workloads
Manage tasks in order of importance when behind
5 P’s Check
Used to evaluate the pilot’s current situation at key decision points during the ﬂight, or when an emergency arises
This is a very helpful portion of Single Pilot Resource Management (SRM)
Based on the idea that the pilot has five variables that impact the environment and can cause the pilot to make a single critical decision, or several less critical decisions, that when added together can create a critical outcome
The process is simple; at least 5 times before/during the flight, review and consider the 5 P’s and make the appropriate decision required by the current situation
The decision points include preflight, pre-takeoff, hourly or at the midpoint of flight, pre-descent, and just prior to the final approach fix or entering the traffic pattern
The 5 P’s:
The Plan
The mission. It contains planning, weather, route, fuel, publication currency, etc.
The plan is always changing (weather changes, delays, restrictions, etc.), adjust with it
The Plane
Condition, abilities (performance, but also automation, database currency, etc.), equipment, systems, etc.
The Pilot
IMSAFE
Allows the pilot to recognize and review his/her physiological situation
The Passengers
Passenger’s desires can have an influence on decision making and risk management
Plan as much as possible
Ensure passengers are involved in decision making process
Ensure they understand risk involved in situations
i.e., IFR approach below minimums or takeoff with IFR below landing minimums
Understand what passengers want to do
They may be more risk averse than you
The Programming
Plan when and where programming approaches/route changes, and airport information gathering should be accomplished, as well as when it should not be accomplished
Pilot familiarity with the equipment, the route, the local air trafﬁc control environment, and personal capabilities should drive when, where, how the automation is programmed and used
Always consider pilot capabilities in relation to programming
Decision Making Process
DECIDE Model (pictured below)
Detect, Estimate, Choose, Identify, Do, Evaluate
Analytical Models
Examples include DECIDE model and 5 Ps
Good decisions result when pilots gather all information, review it, analyze the options, rate the options, select a course of action, and evaluate the course of action for correctness
This level of analysis is not always possible
Automatic or Naturalized Decision Making
Reflexive type of decision making anchored in training and experience
In an emergency, a pilot may not survive if they apply analytical models to every decision
Automatic or Naturalized Process
Experts faced with a task loaded with uncertainty first assess if the situation looks familiar
Rather than comparing pros and cons of different approaches (analytical model), they imagine how one or a few courses of action will play out and take the first workable option they find
May not be the best of all possible choices, but it often works remarkably well
Experienced based actions trigger response to specific situations
Improves with training and experience
Operational Pitfalls (pictured below)
Pitfalls/behavioral traps also come with experience
As a rule, more experienced pilots try to complete flights as planned, please passengers, meet schedules
Can have an adverse effect on safety and contribute to unrealistic assessment of skills
Tendencies must be eliminated
Evaluation
Review and debrief each flight
What went well?
What could have gone better?
What will I (or we) do next time?
Areas to Consider in the Evaluation
Planning & Decision Making
Leadership Effectiveness
Situational Awareness
Communication
Monitor/Cross-Check
Workload Management
Automation Management
Conclusion:
Brief review of the main points

The Airplane as an Energy System
An aircraft’s total mechanical energy is the sum of:
In flight, an airplane is an “Open Energy System”
An airplane can gain energy through thrust & lose energy through drag
Energy can be added or removed from total energy and stored as airspeed or altitude
Energy management involves balancing thrust (T) & drag (D)
If T – D > 0      Total energy increases & can be applied to airspeed or altitude
If T – D < 0      Total energy decreases resulting in a descent or deceleration
If T – D = 0      Energy is constant – airspeed or altitude changes come from trading one for the other
Left side represents the airplane’s Total Energy Flow: Thrust & Drag
Right side reflects the matching changes to Energy Storage: Altitude & Airspeed
Energy is controlled by changing Pitch (elevator) & Power (throttle)
Throttle: Regulates energy by increasing or decreasing thrust
When thrust > drag, total energy increases & vice versa
Elevator: Adjusts energy distribution between altitude & airspeed
Front side of the Power Curve
Point A: High speed, Low AOA, No ability to climb
